cite.hochreiter1997.raw: [13] Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber. Long short-term memory. Neural computation, 9(8):1735–1780, 1997.
cite.hochreiter1997.title: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
cite.hochreiter1997.significance: LSTM introduced gates that control what information to write, keep and use as a recurrent network reads a sequence.
cite.hochreiter1997.connection: LSTM processes a sequence in order, carrying a memory from one position to the next. The authors use it to explain what they changed when they built the Transformer around attention.

cite.gruEval14.raw: [7] Junyoung Chung, Çaglar Gülçehre, Kyunghyun Cho, and Yoshua Bengio. Empirical evaluation of gated recurrent neural networks on sequence modeling. CoRR, abs/1412.3555, 2014.
cite.gruEval14.title: Empirical Evaluation of Gated Recurrent Neural Networks on Sequence Modeling
cite.gruEval14.significance: The authors compared two ways recurrent networks control which information to keep as they read a sequence, the GRU and the LSTM.
cite.gruEval14.connection: Gated recurrent networks carry information forward one position at a time. The authors cite them when explaining why they chose attention for parallel processing.

cite.sutskever14.raw: [35] Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals, and Quoc VV Le. Sequence to sequence learning with neural networks. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, pages 3104–3112, 2014.
cite.sutskever14.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
cite.sutskever14.significance: An encoder reads the source sentence and a decoder generates the translation. This study demonstrated that the two could be trained together.
cite.sutskever14.connection: In both models, an encoder processes the input and a decoder produces the translation. The Transformer changes how those two parts process the sequence.

cite.bahdanau2014neural.raw: [2] Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, and Yoshua Bengio. Neural machine translation by jointly learning to align and translate. CoRR, abs/1409.0473, 2014.
cite.bahdanau2014neural.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
cite.bahdanau2014neural.significance: When predicting each translated word, the decoder computed weights for the source positions and used a weighted combination of their information.
cite.bahdanau2014neural.connection: This earlier translator used attention to find relevant words in the input. The Transformer makes attention the main way to connect positions and removes the recurrent layers.

cite.cho2014learning.raw: [5] Kyunghyun Cho, Bart van Merrienboer, Caglar Gulcehre, Fethi Bougares, Holger Schwenk, and Yoshua Bengio. Learning phrase representations using rnn encoder-decoder for statistical machine translation. CoRR, abs/1406.1078, 2014.
cite.cho2014learning.title: Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation
cite.cho2014learning.significance: The authors trained one recurrent network to encode a phrase and another to predict a translation from that encoding.
cite.cho2014learning.connection: Both models encode source text and then generate a translation. The Transformer uses attention where the earlier network processed tokens in sequence.

cite.wu2016google.raw: [38] Yonghui Wu, Mike Schuster, Zhifeng Chen, Quoc V Le, Mohammad Norouzi, Wolfgang Macherey, Maxim Krikun, Yuan Cao, Qin Gao, Klaus Macherey, et al. Google’s neural machine translation system: Bridging the gap between human and machine translation. arXiv preprint arXiv:1609.08144, 2016.
cite.wu2016google.title: Google’s Neural Machine Translation System
cite.wu2016google.significance: The report describes how a large translation system was trained and how it chose a translation from several candidates.
cite.wu2016google.connection: The authors compare translation quality with this earlier system. When discussing decoding, they also credit it for a way to adjust candidate scores for length.

cite.luong2015effective.raw: [24] Minh-Thang Luong, Hieu Pham, and Christopher D Manning. Effective approaches to attentionbased neural machine translation. arXiv preprint arXiv:1508.04025, 2015.
cite.luong2015effective.title: Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
cite.luong2015effective.significance: The authors compared translation models that attend to the whole source sentence with models that focus on a smaller region.
cite.luong2015effective.connection: Earlier translation models combined recurrent layers with attention. The authors cite those experiments to explain and compare their own use of attention throughout the model.

cite.jozefowicz2016exploring.raw: [15] Rafal Jozefowicz, Oriol Vinyals, Mike Schuster, Noam Shazeer, and Yonghui Wu. Exploring the limits of language modeling. arXiv preprint arXiv:1602.02410, 2016.
cite.jozefowicz2016exploring.title: Exploring the Limits of Language Modeling
cite.jozefowicz2016exploring.significance: The authors tested which training and design choices helped large recurrent networks predict the next word.
cite.jozefowicz2016exploring.connection: The cited study reports how well a large recurrent model predicts language. The authors use this earlier result as context for a design that permits more parallel work.

cite.Kuchaiev2017Factorization.raw: [21] Oleksii Kuchaiev and Boris Ginsburg. Factorization tricks for LSTM networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:1703.10722, 2017.
cite.Kuchaiev2017Factorization.title: Factorization Tricks for LSTM Networks
cite.Kuchaiev2017Factorization.significance: The researchers expressed large LSTM weight matrices as products of smaller matrices to reduce computation.
cite.Kuchaiev2017Factorization.connection: This work made recurrent layers cheaper to compute. The Transformer authors point out that each position still has to wait for the previous one.

cite.shazeer2017outrageously.raw: [32] Noam Shazeer, Azalia Mirhoseini, Krzysztof Maziarz, Andy Davis, Quoc Le, Geoffrey Hinton, and Jeff Dean. Outrageously large neural networks: The sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts layer. arXiv preprint arXiv:1701.06538, 2017.
cite.shazeer2017outrageously.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
cite.shazeer2017outrageously.significance: For each input, a router selects a few expert networks to run. The model can therefore store many experts while using only a few at a time.
cite.shazeer2017outrageously.connection: The cited model activates only some parts of a network for each input. The authors mention it as another way to reduce computation.

cite.structuredAttentionNetworks.raw: [19] Yoon Kim, Carl Denton, Luong Hoang, and Alexander M. Rush. Structured attention networks. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2017.
cite.structuredAttentionNetworks.title: Structured Attention Networks
cite.structuredAttentionNetworks.significance: This work built attention mechanisms that can represent relationships with a structure, such as a sequence of connected choices.
cite.structuredAttentionNetworks.connection: The earlier work used attention to represent structured relationships. The authors include it among previous uses of attention in language models.

cite.decomposableAttnModel.raw: [27] Ankur Parikh, Oscar Täckström, Dipanjan Das, and Jakob Uszkoreit. A decomposable attention model. In Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2016.
cite.decomposableAttnModel.title: A Decomposable Attention Model
cite.decomposableAttnModel.significance: The model used attention to compare two sentences when deciding whether one followed from the other.
cite.decomposableAttnModel.connection: The cited model already used attention without a recurrent network for a language task. This gives readers a specific earlier example of that idea.

cite.extendedngpu.raw: [16] Łukasz Kaiser and Samy Bengio. Can active memory replace attention? In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, (NIPS), 2016.
cite.extendedngpu.title: Can Active Memory Replace Attention?
cite.extendedngpu.significance: The authors tested sequence models that repeatedly update a memory while processing the input.
cite.extendedngpu.connection: This earlier model explored how to process several sequence positions at once. It provides another design to compare with the Transformer.

cite.NalBytenet2017.raw: [18] Nal Kalchbrenner, Lasse Espeholt, Karen Simonyan, Aaron van den Oord, Alex Graves, and Koray Kavukcuoglu. Neural machine translation in linear time. arXiv preprint arXiv:1610.10099v2, 2017.
cite.NalBytenet2017.title: Neural Machine Translation in Linear Time (ByteNet)
cite.NalBytenet2017.significance: The authors used convolutional layers so that a translation model could process more input positions at the same time.
cite.NalBytenet2017.connection: In a convolutional network, distant words exchange information through a series of layers. The Transformer authors compare that path with self-attention, which can connect the two positions in one layer.

cite.JonasFaceNet2017.raw: [9] Jonas Gehring, Michael Auli, David Grangier, Denis Yarats, and Yann N. Dauphin. Convolutional sequence to sequence learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.03122v2, 2017.
cite.JonasFaceNet2017.title: Convolutional Sequence to Sequence Learning
cite.JonasFaceNet2017.significance: The authors used convolutional layers to read an input sequence and generate an output sequence, including for translation.
cite.JonasFaceNet2017.connection: This earlier translation model also processes positions in parallel. It offers a comparison for both sequence processing and the way a model encodes word order.

cite.hochreiter2001gradient.raw: [12] Sepp Hochreiter, Yoshua Bengio, Paolo Frasconi, and Jürgen Schmidhuber. Gradient flow in recurrent nets: the difficulty of learning long-term dependencies, 2001.
cite.hochreiter2001gradient.title: Gradient Flow in Recurrent Nets: The Difficulty of Learning Long-Term Dependencies
cite.hochreiter2001gradient.significance: The study explains why gradients can weaken as they pass back through many recurrent steps, making distant relationships hard to learn.
cite.hochreiter2001gradient.connection: This study explains why recurrent networks can struggle to learn links between distant words. Self-attention gives two distant positions a direct connection.

cite.cheng2016long.raw: [4] Jianpeng Cheng, Li Dong, and Mirella Lapata. Long short-term memory-networks for machine reading. arXiv preprint arXiv:1601.06733, 2016.
cite.cheng2016long.title: Long Short-Term Memory-Networks for Machine Reading
cite.cheng2016long.significance: The study tested how attention over earlier words and memory of the text help a network read a passage.
cite.cheng2016long.connection: The cited work used attention between positions in the same text. That earlier result helps explain why the authors chose self-attention as a building block.

cite.paulus2017deep.raw: [28] Romain Paulus, Caiming Xiong, and Richard Socher. A deep reinforced model for abstractive summarization. arXiv preprint arXiv:1705.04304, 2017.
cite.paulus2017deep.title: A Deep Reinforced Model for Abstractive Summarization
cite.paulus2017deep.significance: The authors trained a model to write summaries using attention and rewards for the summaries it generated.
cite.paulus2017deep.connection: The cited study had already used attention to generate summaries. It shows where attention had worked before the Transformer translation experiments.

cite.lin2017structured.raw: [22] Zhouhan Lin, Minwei Feng, Cicero Nogueira dos Santos, Mo Yu, Bing Xiang, Bowen Zhou, and Yoshua Bengio. A structured self-attentive sentence embedding. arXiv preprint arXiv:1703.03130, 2017.
cite.lin2017structured.title: A Structured Self-Attentive Sentence Embedding
cite.lin2017structured.significance: The model used several sets of attention weights to capture different parts of a sentence in its numerical representation.
cite.lin2017structured.connection: The earlier system used self-attention to represent a sentence. The Transformer uses self-attention in its encoder and decoder.

cite.sukhbaatar2015.raw: [34] Sainbayar Sukhbaatar, Arthur Szlam, Jason Weston, and Rob Fergus. End-to-end memory networks. In C. Cortes, N. D. Lawrence, D. D. Lee, M. Sugiyama, and R. Garnett, editors, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 28, pages 2440–2448. Curran Associates, Inc., 2015.
cite.sukhbaatar2015.title: End-to-End Memory Networks
cite.sukhbaatar2015.significance: The network learned where to read from memory as part of learning to answer questions.
cite.sukhbaatar2015.connection: The earlier model used attention to read from memory when answering questions. It is one example of attention being used beyond translation.

cite.neural_gpu.raw: [17] Łukasz Kaiser and Ilya Sutskever. Neural GPUs learn algorithms. In International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2016.
cite.neural_gpu.title: Neural GPUs Learn Algorithms
cite.neural_gpu.significance: The authors tested a network that could process sequence positions in parallel while learning tasks with algorithmic rules.
cite.neural_gpu.connection: Both studies ask how a network can process more of a sequence in parallel. The cited work explores a different network design for that purpose.

cite.graves2013generating.raw: [10] Alex Graves. Generating sequences with recurrent neural networks. arXiv preprint arXiv:1308.0850, 2013.
cite.graves2013generating.title: Generating Sequences with Recurrent Neural Networks
cite.graves2013generating.significance: The study tested recurrent networks that generate a sequence by predicting one new element at each step.
cite.graves2013generating.connection: When generating a translation, the model predicts each new output token from the tokens it has already generated. The cited work used that same generation order.

cite.he2016deep.raw: [11] Kaiming He, Xiangyu Zhang, Shaoqing Ren, and Jian Sun. Deep residual learning for image recognition. In Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pages 770–778, 2016.
cite.he2016deep.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
cite.he2016deep.significance: A residual connection adds a layer's input to its computed output. This helped researchers train much deeper networks.
cite.he2016deep.connection: The Transformer uses the residual connection introduced here. It adds a sublayer's input to its output so information can pass through successive layers.

cite.layernorm2016.raw: [1] Jimmy Lei Ba, Jamie Ryan Kiros, and Geoffrey E Hinton. Layer normalization. arXiv preprint arXiv:1607.06450, 2016.
cite.layernorm2016.title: Layer Normalization
cite.layernorm2016.significance: Layer normalization rescales a layer's activations within each example, helping stabilize training.
cite.layernorm2016.connection: The authors use layer normalization after combining a sublayer's input with its output. This rescales activations during training.

cite.DBLP:journals/corr/BritzGLL17.raw: [3] Denny Britz, Anna Goldie, Minh-Thang Luong, and Quoc V. Le. Massive exploration of neural machine translation architectures. CoRR, abs/1703.03906, 2017.
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/BritzGLL17.title: Massive Exploration of Neural Machine Translation Architectures
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/BritzGLL17.significance: The researchers trained translation models with different design choices and compared the measured results.
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/BritzGLL17.connection: The cited experiments tested several choices for translation models. They provide measured comparisons of different ways to score a match between positions.

cite.press2016using.raw: [30] Ofir Press and Lior Wolf. Using the output embedding to improve language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:1608.05859, 2016.
cite.press2016using.title: Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models
cite.press2016using.significance: The study reused one matrix both to represent input tokens and to score possible output tokens.
cite.press2016using.connection: The Transformer reuses the same weight matrix for representing tokens and for scoring possible output tokens. This work described that sharing technique.

cite.sennrich2015neural.raw: [31] Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch. Neural machine translation of rare words with subword units. arXiv preprint arXiv:1508.07909, 2015.
cite.sennrich2015neural.title: Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units
cite.sennrich2015neural.significance: The method splits rare words into smaller pieces that can also appear in other words, giving the translator reusable units.
cite.sennrich2015neural.connection: The authors use this technique to split words into pieces before training the translator. A rare word can then be represented using familiar pieces.

cite.xception2016.raw: [6] Francois Chollet. Xception: Deep learning with depthwise separable convolutions. arXiv preprint arXiv:1610.02357, 2016.
cite.xception2016.title: Xception: Deep Learning with Depthwise Separable Convolutions
cite.xception2016.significance: The image model split a convolution into separate steps for processing each channel and combining channels.
cite.xception2016.connection: The authors use this image model's convolution technique to compare the computational cost of different layer designs.

cite.kingma2014adam.raw: [20] Diederik Kingma and Jimmy Ba. Adam: A method for stochastic optimization. In ICLR, 2015.
cite.kingma2014adam.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
cite.kingma2014adam.significance: Adam uses recent gradients to adjust the size of each parameter update during training.
cite.kingma2014adam.connection: Adam supplies the rule the authors used to update model parameters during training.

cite.DBLP:journals/corr/ZhouCWLX16.raw: [39] Jie Zhou, Ying Cao, Xuguang Wang, Peng Li, and Wei Xu. Deep recurrent models with fast-forward connections for neural machine translation. CoRR, abs/1606.04199, 2016.
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/ZhouCWLX16.title: Deep Recurrent Models with Fast-Forward Connections for Neural Machine Translation
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/ZhouCWLX16.significance: The translation model added extra connections between recurrent layers so that information could pass through a deep network more easily.
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/ZhouCWLX16.connection: The results table uses this recurrent translation system to show how the Transformer's translation scores compare with earlier systems.

cite.srivastava2014dropout.raw: [33] Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey E Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Ruslan Salakhutdinov. Dropout: a simple way to prevent neural networks from overfitting. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 15(1):1929–1958, 2014.
cite.srivastava2014dropout.title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting
cite.srivastava2014dropout.significance: Dropout randomly sets some activations to zero during training. It can help a model work better on new examples.
cite.srivastava2014dropout.connection: The Transformer uses dropout during training. It randomly sets some activations to zero, which helps the model generalize beyond its training examples.

cite.DBLP:journals/corr/SzegedyVISW15.raw: [36] Christian Szegedy, Vincent Vanhoucke, Sergey Ioffe, Jonathon Shlens, and Zbigniew Wojna. Rethinking the inception architecture for computer vision. CoRR, abs/1512.00567, 2015.
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/SzegedyVISW15.title: Rethinking the Inception Architecture for Computer Vision
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/SzegedyVISW15.significance: The study tested design and training changes for image classification, including spreading a little target probability across alternative labels.
cite.DBLP:journals/corr/SzegedyVISW15.connection: The authors borrow label smoothing. In training, the target assigns a little probability to alternatives instead of assigning all of it to one correct token.

cite.KVparse15.raw: [37] Vinyals & Kaiser, Koo, Petrov, Sutskever, and Hinton. Grammar as a foreign language. In Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2015.
cite.KVparse15.title: Grammar as a Foreign Language
cite.KVparse15.significance: The model reads a sentence and generates a sequence that describes its grammatical structure.
cite.KVparse15.connection: The earlier study represented a sentence's grammatical structure as an output sequence. The authors compare results from that setup with the Transformer's own parsing results.

cite.marcus1993building.raw: [25] Mitchell P Marcus, Mary Ann Marcinkiewicz, and Beatrice Santorini. Building a large annotated corpus of english: The penn treebank. Computational linguistics, 19(2):313–330, 1993.
cite.marcus1993building.title: Building a Large Annotated Corpus of English: The Penn Treebank
cite.marcus1993building.significance: The Penn Treebank provides English sentences annotated with grammatical structure for training and evaluating parsers.
cite.marcus1993building.connection: The Penn Treebank contains sentences annotated with grammatical structure. Those annotations provide reference answers for evaluating the parser.

cite.petrov-EtAl:2006:ACL.raw: [29] Slav Petrov, Leon Barrett, Romain Thibaux, and Dan Klein. Learning accurate, compact, and interpretable tree annotation. In Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on Computational Linguistics and 44th Annual Meeting of the ACL, pages 433–440. ACL, July 2006.
cite.petrov-EtAl:2006:ACL.title: Learning Accurate, Compact, and Interpretable Tree Annotation
cite.petrov-EtAl:2006:ACL.significance: The parser learned finer distinctions within categories on a grammatical tree to improve its analysis of sentences.
cite.petrov-EtAl:2006:ACL.connection: The authors compare the two models on parsing, the task of identifying the grammatical structure of a sentence.

cite.zhu-EtAl:2013:ACL.raw: [40] Muhua Zhu, Yue Zhang, Wenliang Chen, Min Zhang, and Jingbo Zhu. Fast and accurate shift-reduce constituent parsing. In Proceedings of the 51st Annual Meeting of the ACL (Volume 1: Long Papers), pages 434–443. ACL, August 2013.
cite.zhu-EtAl:2013:ACL.title: Fast and Accurate Shift-Reduce Constituent Parsing
cite.zhu-EtAl:2013:ACL.significance: The parser builds a sentence's grammatical structure one decision at a time, either reading another word or joining groups of words.
cite.zhu-EtAl:2013:ACL.connection: This earlier parser supplies a score for the results table. Both systems are evaluated on identifying grammatical structure in sentences.

cite.dyer-rnng:16.raw: [8] Chris Dyer, Adhiguna Kuncoro, Miguel Ballesteros, and Noah A. Smith. Recurrent neural network grammars. In Proc. of NAACL, 2016.
cite.dyer-rnng:16.title: Recurrent Neural Network Grammars
cite.dyer-rnng:16.significance: The model predicts grammatical structure as well as words, combining grammar rules with a recurrent neural network.
cite.dyer-rnng:16.connection: The cited model explicitly represents grammar when parsing sentences. Its score lets readers compare that design with the Transformer's sequence predictions.

cite.huang-harper:2009:EMNLP.raw: [14] Zhongqiang Huang and Mary Harper. Self-training PCFG grammars with latent annotations across languages. In Proceedings of the 2009 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pages 832–841. ACL, August 2009.
cite.huang-harper:2009:EMNLP.title: Self-Training PCFG Grammars with Latent Annotations Across Languages
cite.huang-harper:2009:EMNLP.significance: The researchers trained a parser on its own analyses of additional sentences, using grammar categories with learned subdivisions.
cite.huang-harper:2009:EMNLP.connection: This earlier parser also learned from extra sentences without human annotations. Its score shows how well that approach worked on the same parsing task.

cite.mcclosky-etAl:2006:NAACL.raw: [26] David McClosky, Eugene Charniak, and Mark Johnson. Effective self-training for parsing. In Proceedings of the Human Language Technology Conference of the NAACL, Main Conference, pages 152–159. ACL, June 2006.
cite.mcclosky-etAl:2006:NAACL.title: Effective Self-Training for Parsing
cite.mcclosky-etAl:2006:NAACL.significance: The parser labeled extra sentences itself, then trained on those automatically produced labels.
cite.mcclosky-etAl:2006:NAACL.connection: The cited parser trained on its own analyses of additional sentences. The authors include its score when comparing ways to use extra training text.

cite.multiseq2seq.raw: [23] Minh-Thang Luong, Quoc V. Le, Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals, and Lukasz Kaiser. Multi-task sequence to sequence learning. arXiv preprint arXiv:1511.06114, 2015.
cite.multiseq2seq.title: Multi-task Sequence to Sequence Learning
cite.multiseq2seq.significance: The authors tested whether a network trained on several input-to-output sequence tasks could share what it learned across those tasks.
cite.multiseq2seq.connection: The table includes this earlier model's parsing score. It learned several tasks together, which matters when comparing it with a model trained on parsing alone.

occurrences.excerpt: The two most commonly used attention functions are additive attention [2], and dot-product (multiplicative) attention. Dot-product attention is identical to our algorithm, except for the scaling factor of 1 √dk . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code.
